sources.title: Translocation, genetic structure and homing ability confirm geographic barriers disrupt saltwater crocodile movement and dispersal
sources.scope: ARGOS tracking of five translocated adult males and three controls in the Northern Territory, paired with genetic analyses of coastal nest samples.
sources.license: Creative Commons Attribution License, stated in the article copyright section; the article does not specify a numbered version.
sources.rightsEvidenceLocator: Copyright statement after article citation; Creative Commons Attribution License.
sources.attribution: Fukuda Y, Webb G, Manolis C, Lindner G, Banks S (2019). Translocation, genetic structure and homing ability confirm geographic barriers disrupt saltwater crocodile movement and dispersal. PLoS ONE 14(8):e0205862. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0205862. Claims are paraphrased.

claims.text: The study reports 8,983 N as the taxon-representative bite force at the molariform position for Crocodylus porosus and separately reports a 16,414 N measurement for one individual.
claims.scope: The individual maximum and taxon-representative statistic are distinct; the specimens were sexually mature adults in the comparative collection sample.

claims.text: Five translocated adult males released 100–320 km from capture sites moved at sea in the direction of those sites, but none completed homing around Cobourg Peninsula; one control crocodile later made a 900 km journey over six months and returned.
claims.scope: A small Northern Territory sample; the study also analyzed genetic structure from nests along that coastline.

gaps: No multi-source species dossier is added.
The movement study does not represent females, juveniles, all populations, or every translocation context.
